issues.legal_issue: A gifted property occupied by a tenant is not deemed to pass on the donor’s death where the donees receive the ownership and the possession the nature of the property permits, and the donor’s separate connection with the tenant does not give him a benefit referable to the gift.
material_facts: The donor transferred the property absolutely and irrevocably to two donees while a firm occupied it as a tenant at will.
After the transfer, the firm treated the donees as landlords and credited rent to their accounts in equal shares.
The donor remained a partner of the firm until it was dissolved.
The donor’s partnership-related benefit was unconnected with the property transferred by the gift.
issues.conclusion: The property was not deemed to pass on the donor’s death and could not be included in his estate.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 10 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953, the donee must bona fide assume possession and enjoyment immediately upon the gift and retain them to the entire exclusion of the donor. The second requirement excludes the donor both from the property and from any benefit by contract or otherwise; “otherwise” means a legal obligation or transaction enforceable at law or in equity, while actual enjoyment of the property may breach the first limb even without an enforceable right. Possession is assessed in light of the nature of the property and the circumstances, and a benefit from a relationship independent of the gift is not a benefit referable to the gift. The Court followed George Da Costa v. Controller of Estate Duty, referred to Munro v. Commissioner of Stamp Duties, Clifford John Chick v. Commissioner of Stamp Duties and Commissioner of Stamp Duties of New South Wales v. Perpetual Trustee Company Ltd., and approved Controller of Estate Duty v. S. Aswathanarayana Setty.

predicates.estate_inclusion_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether gifted property is to be included in a donor’s estate as passing on death.
predicates.gift_effected_unequivocally: The donor transferred the property to the donees without reserving ownership of it.
predicates.donees_received_property_rights_and_avai: The donees received the property rights and the possession available in light of the property’s existing occupation or other circumstances.
predicates.donor_connection_benefit_unconnected_to_: The donor obtained a benefit through a separate relationship or activity, rather than through the property or a transaction arising from the gift.

issues.definition: When an estate-inclusion proceeding concerns an unequivocal gift, the donees receive the property rights and available possession, and the donor’s separate benefit is unconnected to the gift, the property is not deemed to pass.

issues.legal_issue: Money gifted by transfer to the donees’ accounts is not deemed to pass on the donor’s death where the donees become entitled to the credited amounts and the donor’s connection with the firm holding the money does not give him a benefit referable to the gift.
material_facts: The donor instructed the firm to transfer five sums from his account to the accounts of his five sons, and informed them of the transfers.
The firm credited the sums to the sons’ accounts and became liable to them for the amounts and interest.
The sons left the money invested in the firm and did not withdraw it.
The donor remained a partner in the firm, which used the funds, but the donor’s partnership benefit was not referable to the gifts.
issues.conclusion: The gifted sum was not deemed to pass on the donor’s death and could not be included in his estate.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 10 of the Estate Duty Act, 1953, the donee must bona fide assume possession and enjoyment immediately upon the gift and retain them to the entire exclusion of the donor. The second requirement excludes the donor both from the property and from any benefit by contract or otherwise; “otherwise” means a legal obligation or transaction enforceable at law or in equity, while actual enjoyment of the property may breach the first limb even without an enforceable right. A completed transfer that makes the firm liable to the donees can give them possession and enjoyment even if they leave the funds invested there. A benefit arising from the donor’s partnership, rather than from the gift, is not a benefit referable to the gift. The Court followed George Da Costa v. Controller of Estate Duty, referred to Munro v. Commissioner of Stamp Duties, Clifford John Chick v. Commissioner of Stamp Duties and Commissioner of Stamp Duties of New South Wales v. Perpetual Trustee Company Ltd., and approved Controller of Estate Duty v. S. Aswathanarayana Setty.

rule.if: estate_inclusion_proceeding and money_gift_transferred_to_donees and firm_became_liable_to_donees_for_money and donor_connection_benefit_unconnected_to_gift

predicates.estate_inclusion_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether gifted property is to be included in a donor’s estate as passing on death.
predicates.money_gift_transferred_to_donees: The donor transferred money to the donees, including by crediting it to accounts held for them.
predicates.firm_became_liable_to_donees_for_money: The firm holding the credited money became liable to pay the amounts and any agreed return to the donees.
predicates.donor_connection_benefit_unconnected_to_: The donor obtained a benefit through a separate relationship or activity, rather than through the money or a transaction arising from the gift.

issues.definition: When an estate-inclusion proceeding concerns money transferred to the donees, the firm holding it becomes liable to them, and the donor’s separate benefit is unconnected to the gift, the money is not deemed to pass.
